sections.overview: Acicula fusca is a minute land snail in the family Aciculidae. Its common English name, point snail, refers to the tapered shell. Because it is only a few millimetres long and lives in concealed ground-level microhabitats, it is easily overlooked during ordinary wildlife searches.
sections.identification: The adult shell is tiny, reaching about 2.5 mm high and 0.8 mm wide. It is glossy and reddish to yellowish brown, with a blunt apex, a nearly cylindrical taper, fine radial striae and a minute translucent operculum. In Ireland it may be confused with the blind awl snail, Cecilioides acicula, whose shell is smoother and more sharply tapered and lacks this visible operculum. The cited records measure the shell only; no reliable body-mass figure is reported.
sections.habitat: The species occurs in western and central parts of Europe, including Britain, Ireland, France, Spain, Belgium and northwestern Germany. It is associated with moist leaf litter and moss in broadleaf woodland and other base-rich, well-soiled sites. Irish conservation sources also record it in rough grassland and hedgerow settings with rich deep soil; habitat descriptions vary by locality.
sections.diet: The reviewed species accounts focus on shell characters and habitat and do not provide direct observations of what A. fusca eats. Its species-specific diet is therefore left undetermined in this profile.
sections.behavior: Its tiny size and concealed life in litter, moss and soil make it difficult to observe alive. The species account from Northern Ireland notes adults can be found throughout the year. The available sources do not describe its movement, activity rhythm or interactions in enough detail for a fuller behavioral account.
sections.reproduction: The Northern Ireland species account notes that adults have separate sexes, unlike most non-marine snails, which are hermaphroditic. Detailed information on courtship, egg laying, development and generation length was not available in the sources reviewed, so those details remain uncertain.
sections.ecology: The point snail is associated with damp, base-rich litter and soil microhabitats, and its minute body makes it a component of the largely unseen soil and litter fauna. The reviewed sources do not quantify its ecological function or interactions with plants, fungi or predators.
sections.conservation: An Irish assessment lists A. fusca as a species of conservation concern and describes it as a British-Irish near endemic with smaller continental populations. The material reviewed here does not establish a current global Red List category or a recent population trend. Loss or degradation of moist, base-rich litter habitat is relevant to the habitat it occupies, but no causal population estimate is supplied.
